cur:objects-berlin-trier-moses-thomas-di.summary: On the left leaf Moses reaches up to receive the tablets of the Law from the hand of God; on the right the risen Christ, standing in a doorway, lifts his arm to reveal the wound in his side as Thomas reaches out to touch it. The two tall, slender figures in rich architectural frames set the Old Covenant beside the New. Christ's gesture offers the doubting apostle — and every viewer — tangible proof of the Resurrection.
facts: The Bode-Museum acquired the two leaves in 1935 (inv. nos. 8505/8506); they are attributed to Trier at the end of the 10th century, when Archbishop Egbert made the city a leading artistic centre.
Pairing Moses receiving the Law with Thomas touching Christ's wound sets the giving of the Old Law beside the revelation of the risen Lord (typological reading).

cur:objects-bm-raising-of-lazarus-ivory.summary: Christ strides forward with an apostle behind him, his hand extended toward the tomb, where Lazarus stands upright in his grave-clothes inside an arched niche; one of the sisters kneels at Christ's feet. Buildings of the town of Bethany rise in the background. The slim panel captures the instant of Christ's command, 'Lazarus, come forth'.
facts: The British Museum catalogues the plaque as Byzantine Empire or Italy (Venice?), about 900–1000, showing that the attribution of such ivories between Byzantium and its Italian imitators can be difficult.

cur:objects-golden-altar-sant-ambrogio.summary: At the centre of the golden front of the high altar Christ is enthroned in a cross-shaped frame, surrounded by the symbols of the evangelists and the twelve apostles; panels on either side narrate the life of Christ, from the Annunciation and Nativity to miracles, the Crucifixion, Resurrection and Ascension. Gems and enamels set into filigree frames make the altar a shining reliquary-like casing. It is one of the supreme achievements of Carolingian goldsmiths' work, still in use over the relics of St Ambrose.
facts: Italian Wikipedia notes that it was made between 824 and 859 for Bishop Angilbert II and is signed by 'Vuolvino magister phaber' (Wolvinius), hence also called the Altar of Volvinio.
It stands over the relics of Saints Gervasius, Protasius and Ambrose, which can still be seen through a small window from the crypt.
